summary: Brick tower on a Mississippi Sound island, built 1859 to replace an 1833 light; toppled by Hurricane George in 1998 and rebuilt on the Pascagoula mainland.

lens.where: Removed with the other equipment at decommissioning in 1944.

structures.note: 50 ft (15 m) per the 1955 federal property report used in the nomination; other sources say 60 ft (18 m). Toppled in 1998; base and remnants moved to Lighthouse Park, Pascagoula, in 2010; restored and opened in 2015.
First tower on the island, replaced by the 1859 brick tower.
Round Island South Spit Light, a separate beacon on the spit to the south; the Board's list of lights for 1900 gives a 'Round Island Spit beacon light' dated 15 February 1900.

staffing.note: The marker says the light was automated around 1940; the roster lists a first assistant at the station from 1940 to 1944.

access.note: Lighthouse Park, 815 Cypress Avenue, Pascagoula. The city lists Friday and Saturday hours, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

events.note: Congress authorized $7,000 for a light off Pascagoula Bay.
First tower; the nomination names the contractor, the marker gives the cost ($5,895).
Board report, as quoted in the nomination: the tower 'badly built' and liable to be undermined.
Board report, as quoted in the nomination: the tower exposed to destruction from the sea in an easterly storm.
Congress authorized $8,000 for the rebuild.
Brick tower built to replace the 1833 tower; the marker gives $7,130.97.
Gale of Monday 2 October 1893; the paper reports only the loss of the quarantine sloop and the wharf at Round Island.
Board report FY1900: 'Round Island Spit beacon light' among the new lights of the year; first shown 15 February 1900 (report item 1027).
Round Island South Spit Light collided with and destroyed by the tug Catherine, 29 March 1916; owners of the tug paid the repairs ($1,184.49).
March 1917: keeper John H. Portman and assistant Frederick A. Schrieber bring seven people from a disabled launch to the station.
5 May 1917: Schrieber assists a leaking small sailing boat near the station and tows it to harbour.
Late February or early March 1920: W. V. LeJune's fishing launch sinks off Horn Island; he and a companion are taken in by the keeper at Round Island.
16 February 1921: keeper Harry Brouwer assists the disabled auxiliary boat A. H. Daughdrill, which had grounded in fog; assistant D. C. Powell helps float it.
17 February 1921: assistant Dewitt C. Powell helps tow a disabled skiff with one occupant to the station.
Fiscal 1922: Brouwer and Powell assist a disabled launch with 10 persons aboard that had drifted near the station.
25 January 1925: Brouwer tows the disabled fishing launch Raich to Pascagoula.
10 August 1926: keeper A. E. Steiner and assistant Tony Ryan assist a fishing party whose boat was disabled near the South Spit Beacon.
Decommissioned as an operational light on 20 March 1944.
Lens removed with the other equipment at decommissioning.
Keeper's dwelling gutted by fire, 24 February 1951.
Keeper's dwelling destroyed by a second fire, August 1954.
Coast Guard day-beacon service ends: 19 September 1954 per the nomination; 1945 per the marker. Not resolved.
General Services Administration declares the property excess to Coast Guard needs.
Deeded to the City of Pascagoula.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places.
Toppled by Hurricane George.
Hurricane Katrina; the marker says it ended any hope of restoring the tower on the island.
City barges the base and remnants to the mainland with grant money.
Restoration completed; tower open to the public at Lighthouse Park.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination and the marker agree on 20 March 1944 for the end of operation. They differ on the end of the Coast Guard day-beacon service (19 September 1954 in the nomination, 1945 in the marker); the story gives both. The station record's other date (1949) is supported by no source read and is not used.
The nomination uses 50 ft from the 1955 excess-property report and notes that various sources give 60 ft. The story reports both.
The marker says automated around 1940; the roster lists a first assistant at the station from 1940 to 1944. The story reports both and does not resolve the question.

The Pascagoula Democrat-Star says the gale struck on Monday the 2nd. The Board's report for fiscal 1894 gives the storm as 'October 1, 1893' in its entries for two beacons at the Pascagoula River mouth. The story states both.

notes_for_editor: (1) Roster match: the USLHS place 'Round Island MS' sits about 42 km from the station record's coordinates (the place record says 'not existing'); it was matched by name and by its keeper list, which agrees with the Board and Commissioner reports (Murray 1893, Portman, Schrieber, Brouwer, Powell, Steiner, Ryan). Recheck against the NARA registers before publishing the person links. (2) Schrieber: roster has him principal 1917-1920 and 1st assistant 1916-1917; the Commissioner's 1917 report calls him assistant keeper, and the Bulletin does the same in May 1917. (3) Unresolved: day-beacon end 1954 (nomination) vs 1945 (marker); tower height 50 ft (1955 report) vs 60 ft; automated c.1940 (marker) vs roster keepers to 1944. The nomination attributes the 1833 contract to the Lighthouse Board; the story leaves the contracting authority open. (4) Pre-1890 Board reports are not in the local corpus; the 1854-1856 Board statements are cited as quoted in the nomination. (5) Sam Maddox from the nomination is not on the roster. (6) OCR: the 1893 paper prints 'Kouhd Island' for Round Island; the 1917 Bulletin's rescue date is OCR-damaged ('Marcb 1.6'), so the story says March 1917. The 1920 LeJune article is undated beyond its 5 March 1920 issue. (7) The 1921 Commissioner volume spells the boat 'Daugherill'; the Bulletin spells it 'Daughdrill' (used). (8) The Bulletin indexes (1912-17) list 'hurricane damage' at Round Island at pages 185 and 225 of that volume; those pages were not read, so no hurricane is described here. (9) The station record's characteristic 'Fl W 2.5s' and range are not supported by any source read here and are not used. (10) The Lighthouse Digest quotation is limited to one short phrase; the HMDB marker text is quoted only as the inscription. (11) No photos proposed. (12) Fact-check 2026-10-22: the USLHS record 'Round Island MS' (30 29.19 N, 88 58.67 W, 'Existing: No') lies about 42 km from the marker's position (30 22.236 N, 88 33.371 W). Its keeper list matches the 1893 paper and the Board, Commissioner and Bulletin reports for the names those print (Murray, Portman, Schrieber, Brouwer, Powell, Steiner, Ryan), so the station identity is corroborated, but the person slugs rest on the USLHS record alone: confirm against NARA before linking. (13) Matched by column position in an OCR'd table: Schrieber's assistant-keeper rank in the FY1917 Commissioner report ('Saving of Life and Property ... Fiscal Year 1917 - Continued', bound-volume scan p.269, printed p.58; the name appears twice, as 'F. A. Schrieber' and 'F. A. Schreilwr'). The page image was not read. (14) The 1854-1855 Board statements are read as the nomination quotes them; the Board's own reports for those years are not in the corpus. (15) The Board's FY1900 list of new lights is cited for the name; the first-shown date comes from the report's item 1027 (scan p.151).
